skills.name: Calculate the percentage yield of a reaction

note.text:
Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 per cent.
To work one out:
1. Find the moles of the limiting reagent.
2. Use the equation to find the moles of product expected.
3. Change that to a mass: this is the theoretical yield.
4. Divide the actual yield by it and multiply by 100.
A yield above 100 per cent is impossible; if one is calculated, the product is probably still wet or impure.
Yields matter in industry: a low yield wastes raw material, so the cost of the reactants, the energy used and the purity of the product are all weighed up together when a process is chosen.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to calculate a percentage yield from experimental masses and explain why yields fall short.
Builds on: Lesson {26} (theoretical yield and limiting reagents) and Lesson {25} (masses from equations).
Leads to: Lesson {28} (balancing by the mole concept) and the costing of industrial processes.

sections.heading: Working out a percentage yield

key_words.meaning: the mass of product really collected
the mass once no more water can be driven off

examples: {4.4} g of a possible {5.6} g: {78.6} per cent
{8} g of a possible {10} g: {80} per cent

mistake.wrong: a yield of {110} per cent shows an unusually good reaction
mistake.right: it shows the product was wet or impure
mistake.why: Atoms are conserved, so no reaction can beat its theoretical yield.

worked_example.problem: {m} g of calcium carbonate is heated and {y} g of calcium oxide is collected. Find the percentage yield.

example: {8} g collected out of a possible {10} g is {80} per cent

cards.idea: Work out the theoretical yield from the equation first.

check.prompt: What is the theoretical mass, in grams, of magnesium oxide from burning {m} g of magnesium completely?

misconceptions.explain: Oxygen adds to the mass, so the oxide is heavier than the magnesium.
The ratio is {2} : {2}, that is {1} mol of oxide for each {1} mol of magnesium.

solution: {2}Mg + {formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('MgO')}: {1} mol of Mg gives {1} mol of {formula('MgO')}.

cards.idea: A yield above {100} per cent means the product is wet or impure.
example: dry the product to constant mass before weighing it

check.prompt: A reaction has a theoretical yield of {t} g. A pupil weighs the product and finds {y} g. By what mass, in grams, must the product be wet or impure?

misconceptions.explain: Find the DIFFERENCE between what was weighed and what was possible.
That is the percentage yield; the question asks for a mass in grams.

solution: No reaction can give more than its theoretical yield of {t} g.
The extra mass must be water or impurity: {y} − {t} = {answer} g.

pick.q: Why can a percentage yield never be more than {100} per cent?
pick.r: No more product can be made than the equation allows from the reactants used
w: Because the balance is not accurate enough
Because some reactant is always left over
It can be more than {100} per cent in a good experiment
e: A more accurate balance would not create extra product.
Leftover reactant lowers the yield, it does not raise it.
A figure above {100} per cent means the product is wet or impure.
pick.y: Atoms are conserved: the theoretical yield already counts every atom available.

pick.q: A pupil calculates a percentage yield of {110} per cent. What is the most likely reason?
pick.r: The product was weighed before it was dry, so the water counted as product
w: The balance was set to zero
The theoretical yield was too large
e: No reaction can beat its theoretical yield.
Zeroing the balance is correct practice and would not raise the mass.
A theoretical yield that was too large would give a yield BELOW {100} per cent.
pick.y: Water or unreacted material left in the product adds to the mass weighed.

pick.q: Which of these lowers the percentage yield?
pick.r: Some of the product stays on the filter paper
w: Using excess of the other reactant
e: A cleaner balance gives a more accurate reading, not a lower yield.
A correct equation gives the right theoretical yield.
Excess of the other reactant does not change what the limiting reagent can give.
pick.y: Any product left behind in the apparatus is not weighed, so the actual yield falls.

pick.q: Why does industry care about percentage yield?
pick.r: A low yield wastes raw material and money, so the process may not be worth running
w: A low yield makes the product impure
A low yield makes the reaction dangerous
Yield has nothing to do with cost
e: Purity and yield are different measurements.
A low yield is wasteful, not necessarily dangerous.
Raw materials cost money, so the yield is central to the cost.
pick.y: If only half the reactant becomes product, twice as much must be bought for the same output.

pick.q: Two methods make the same product. One has a yield of {85} per cent and the other {40} per cent. What else must be known before choosing?
pick.r: The cost and availability of the reactants, the energy needed and how pure the product is
w: Nothing: always choose the higher yield
Only the colour of the product
Only how long each method takes
e: A high yield from a very expensive reactant can still be the worse choice.
Colour is not usually what decides a process.
Time matters, but so do cost, energy and purity.
pick.y: Yield is one factor among several in choosing an industrial process.
